intro/hello: This lecture is about a simple idea that reshaped post-training in 2025: rewards a program can check.
intro/recap: R L H F trains a reward model on human comparisons, then optimizes against it. D P O fits the comparisons directly.
intro/guess: Either way, the reward is a learned guess, and a policy that optimizes hard against a guess finds where it is wrong.
intro/check: For some tasks we can do better: a math answer can be checked, and a program can be tested.
intro/rlvr: Use the checker as the reward, and you get reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: R L V R.
intro/grpo: Pair it with G R P O, a lean version of P P O with no value network, and you have the recipe behind DeepSeek R one.
intro/plan: We will build it piece by piece: verifiers, a P P O recap, G R P O term by term, a toy trained live, the R one recipes, and how G R P O goes wrong.
verifier/q: A question with a known answer: four thirty seven plus two eighty five.
verifier/out: The model reasons, then puts its final answer in a box.
verifier/extract: The verifier is a few lines of code. It pulls out what is in the box,
verifier/compare: compares it with the stored answer, seven twenty two, and returns one on a match, zero if not.
verifier/wrong: A wrong answer gets zero. So does an answer with no box at all: the format is part of the task.
verifier/binary: The reward is binary, cheap and exact. It grades the answer, never the reasoning.
verifier/rm: A reward model is a network, and networks have adversarial inputs: strange outputs that score high.
verifier/fool: Optimize long enough and the policy finds them: reward hacking.
verifier/robust: A checker that compares a number with seven twenty two has no such blind spot. The only way to earn its reward is to be right.
verifier/name: The name R L V R comes from A I two's Tulu three, in 2024. DeepSeek calls the same thing rule-based rewards.
gaming/still: Verifiable rewards are hard to hack, not impossible. The policy optimizes what the checker checks, not what you meant.
gaming/six: Here are six answers to one question, each marked with a careful human's verdict.
gaming/anybox: Suppose the checker accepts any boxed answer that matches. Then boxing two guesses earns full reward.
gaming/anynum: Accept any number in the text, and spraying numbers works too.
gaming/strict: A strict checker wants exactly one box, compared as a number. Both exploits fail, and seven twenty two point zero still passes.
gaming/partial: The second gap is a partial checker. Three unit tests reward any code that passes them,
gaming/cheat: including code that simply memorizes them.
gaming/answer: And a checker that reads only the final answer gives full credit to a lucky guess.
gaming/lesson: So treat the verifier as training code, and test it against adversarial outputs before a long run.
ppo/policy: First, a recap of P P O, which G R P O mostly keeps. A language model is a policy: it picks each next token with some probability.
ppo/pg: The policy gradient raises the probability of outputs that did better than expected, and lowers the rest.
ppo/adv: Better than expected is the advantage, A hat: the reward minus a baseline, an estimate of what the model usually gets.
ppo/reuse: P P O takes several steps on each sampled batch, weighting each token by a ratio, rho: its probability now, over when it was sampled.
ppo/ratio: A ratio of one means unchanged. One point three means the token is now thirty percent more likely.
ppo/clip: Then it clips. For a good token, the objective rises with the ratio until one plus epsilon, then goes flat.
ppo/flat: Flat means zero gradient: the token stops being pushed. Bad tokens get the same treatment below one minus epsilon.
ppo/safe: So one batch cannot move the policy far.
ppo/critic: P P O's advantage comes from a critic: a value network that predicts, at every token, the reward still to come.
ppo/four: So P P O holds four models: the policy and the critic, both trained, plus a frozen reference and reward model.
ppo/heavy: The critic is as big as the policy, and must predict a reward that only arrives at the end. G R P O throws it away.
group/idea: Group Relative Policy Optimization comes from DeepSeekMath, in 2024. Its idea fits in one sentence.
group/sentence: Instead of training a critic to guess how well the model does, sample several answers and look.
group/sample: For each question, draw a group of G outputs. Here are eight, from a toy model doing addition.
group/tokens: Blue chips are steps of work, orange chips re-check the work, and the purple chip is the final answer.
group/verify: The verifier scores each one. Two of the eight are right.
group/mean: The average reward, one quarter, is the model's pass rate on this question: exactly what a critic would try to learn.
group/adv: Each output's advantage is its reward minus that mean, divided by the group's standard deviation.
group/values: The two right answers get plus one point seven three. The six wrong ones get minus point five eight.
group/sum: The advantages always add up to zero, so probability moves from worse outputs to better ones.
group/broadcast: And every token of an output gets that same advantage: the whole row is pushed up, or down.
group/hard: On a hard question, a rare right answer earns a big advantage. On an easy one, being right earns little.
group/cost: The price is G samples per question, which reasoning training pays for anyway.
objective/whole: Here is the whole G R P O objective. It looks dense, but it is P P O's with two swaps. Let us read it piece by piece.
objective/group: Outside, one over G times a sum over i: an average over the group.
objective/tokens: Inside, one over the length of output i, times a sum over its tokens: an average over that output's tokens. Remember this one.
objective/ratio: For each token, the ratio rho: its probability now, over when it was sampled.
objective/adv: Times A hat, the group advantage, the same for every token of the output.
objective/clip: Then P P O's clip and min, unchanged.
objective/kl: And minus beta times a K L penalty, which keeps the policy near the frozen reference model, pi ref.
objective/inloss: P P O folds that penalty into the reward. G R P O adds it to the loss, so the advantage stays a clean function of the rewards.
objective/estimator: The penalty uses a neat estimator. Let x be the reference's probability of the sampled token, over the policy's.
objective/curve: Then x minus log x minus one is zero when the two agree, and positive everywhere else.
objective/unbiased: Averaged over samples it equals the true K L divergence, and it is never negative, which keeps it low in noise.
objective/code: In code, it is about ten lines: ratio, clip, penalty, and two averages.
memory/bytes: How much does the critic cost? Training with Adam in mixed precision takes about sixteen bytes per parameter.
memory/split: Two for the weights, two for the gradients, four for a full-precision copy, and eight for Adam's two running averages.
memory/frozen: A frozen model that only runs inference needs two bytes per parameter.
memory/ppo: So at seven billion parameters each, P P O's four models need about two hundred and fifty gigabytes, before a single activation.
memory/grpo: G R P O drops the critic: a hundred and twelve gigabytes gone, as much as the policy itself.
memory/rlvr: With a verifier, the reward model goes too. That is half of P P O's memory.
memory/compute: It also saves the critic's compute, freeing room for generation: long answers, many per prompt.
toy/world: Let us watch G R P O work on a toy you can train in the chapter. The prompt is an addition problem of one to four digits.
toy/vocab: It has three tokens: work out the next column, check the work so far, or write the answer.
toy/slips: A column slips fifteen percent of the time, a check fixes a slip seventy percent of the time, and unworked columns are guessed.
toy/base: The base model answers too early and rarely checks. It is right about thirty percent of the time.
toy/train: Now train: groups of eight, eight problems per batch, two clipped passes each.
toy/acc: Accuracy climbs, from about thirty percent to nearly ninety.
toy/len: And something nobody asked for: the outputs get longer, from under three tokens to over five.
toy/why: Working every column, and spending a token on a check, pays off. Most of the new length is that useful work.
toy/filler: Some is filler: work after the last column, which no reward discourages. Remember that.
toy/checks: And the check tokens multiply. Self-verification appeared because it raised the reward.
toy/r1: Longer outputs, more checking, higher accuracy: the pattern DeepSeek saw at enormous scale.
r1zero/jan: In January 2025, DeepSeek released R one, and with it an experiment called R one Zero.
r1zero/nosft: R one Zero is G R P O applied straight to the pretrained DeepSeek V three Base, with no supervised fine-tuning.
r1zero/template: A simple template asks it to reason inside think tags, then answer.
r1zero/rewards: The reward is a rule: an answer check for math, test cases for code, and a format check. No reward model.
r1zero/aime: On the A I M E 2024 math contest, the paper reports single-sample accuracy rising from fifteen point six to seventy one percent.
r1zero/vote: With a majority vote over sixty four samples, eighty six point seven percent.
r1zero/long: And, like our toy, its answers grew steadily longer, from hundreds of tokens toward many thousands.
r1zero/aha: Reflection emerged too. The paper shows a checkpoint writing, mid-solution: wait, wait. wait. that's an aha moment I can flag here. Then it re-checks its work.
r1zero/flaws: But R one Zero's reasoning was hard to read, and it mixed languages inside a single answer.
r1/stages: R one keeps the RL and wraps it in stages, starting again from the same base.
r1/cold: Stage one, a cold start: fine-tune on a few thousand long, readable chains of thought.
r1/rl1: Stage two: the same reasoning RL as R one Zero, plus a reward for staying in one language.
r1/rs: Stage three: sample from that model and keep the good answers, about six hundred thousand, plus two hundred thousand ordinary assistant examples.
r1/sft: Fine-tune the base again on those eight hundred thousand, for two epochs.
r1/rl2: Stage four: a last RL round over all prompts, with rules where answers can be checked and reward models elsewhere. That is R one.
r1/distill: Then the cheapest step, distillation: fine-tune smaller open models, one and a half to seventy billion parameters, on the same samples. No RL.
r1/strong: They reason far better than the models they started from.
r1/vsrl: And RL run directly on a thirty-two billion parameter base did much worse than distilling R one into that size.
r1/lesson: Reasoning that a huge model discovers through RL can be handed to a small model with ordinary fine-tuning.
biases/edges: G R P O's simplicity hides sharp edges, and the open reproductions of R one Zero kept hitting the same four.
biases/zero: First, groups with no signal. If all eight outputs are right, or all wrong, every advantage is zero.
biases/worse: That question wastes compute, and it gets worse as training succeeds: mastered questions become all-right groups.
biases/dyn: D A P O's fix is dynamic sampling: drop those groups and refill the batch.
biases/len: Second, length. Averaging over each output's tokens makes each token's weight the advantage divided by the length.
biases/right: Among right answers, short ones get a bigger push per token.
biases/wrong: Among wrong answers, long ones get a smaller penalty per token: length softens the blow.
biases/drgrpo: The Doctor G R P O paper, G R P O done right, argues this lets wrong answers grow ever longer. Its fix: divide by one constant.
biases/std: Third, difficulty. Dividing by the standard deviation rescales each question, and it is small when nearly everything is right, or wrong.
biases/weight: So those get inflated: a question solved seven times in eight pulls two thirds as hard as a fifty-fifty one. Without the division, less than half.
biases/drfix: Doctor G R P O drops that division too, leaving an honest policy gradient with the group mean as baseline.
entropy/entropy: Fourth, entropy collapse. Entropy measures how spread out the policy's choices are, and under RL it falls fast, even in our toy.
entropy/same: A confident policy writes near-identical outputs, which get identical rewards: no signal, and no exploration.
entropy/blame: The D A P O authors traced part of this to the clip itself.
entropy/ratio: The clip limits the ratio, so how far a token can move in one batch is proportional to where it started.
entropy/likely: A token at probability point nine may rise all the way to one: no real limit.
entropy/rare: A token at point zero one may only reach point zero one two. Rare tokens, which open new lines of reasoning, can barely grow.
entropy/higher: The fix, clip higher, raises only the top of the band: D A P O uses point two below and point two eight above.
entropy/dapo: D A P O bundles four changes: clip higher, dynamic sampling, a loss averaged over every token in the batch, and gentler handling of truncated answers.
entropy/nokl: It also drops the K L penalty, so long reasoning training can move the policy far from where it began.
entropy/result: From a thirty-two billion parameter base it reached about fifty on A I M E, beating the R one paper's RL result there in half the steps.
outro/rlvr: To sum up. Verifiable rewards replace a learned reward model with a program, far harder to hack if the checker is strict.
outro/grpo: G R P O is P P O without the critic: sample a group, use its mean as the baseline, give every token its output's advantage, and clip.
outro/mem: Dropping the critic halves the memory, and samples you were going to draw anyway do the critic's job.
outro/r1: R one Zero showed this alone grows long reasoning and self-checking. R one made it readable; distillation handed it down.
outro/fail: And the sharp edges have names: no-signal groups, length and difficulty bias, entropy collapse. Doctor G R P O and D A P O fix them.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter: train the toy yourself, break a verifier, and drag the clip. See you there.
